title: Codependency test: am I codependent? Free quiz — cv.cm
description: Free codependency test: rate 14 statements about people-pleasing, saying no and putting others first to get a score from 0 to 56, what it means and how to build healthier boundaries. Not a diagnosis. Answers stay in your browser.
lede: Do you feel responsible for everyone's feelings, find it hard to say no, or lose yourself in a relationship? Rate 14 statements to see how strongly codependent patterns show up in your life.
about: Codependency describes a pattern of putting other people's needs, moods and problems so far ahead of your own that you lose track of what you want and feel. The term first came from families affected by alcohol addiction, where partners and children often took on the job of keeping everyone else afloat. Today it is used more widely for relationships where your sense of worth depends on being needed, where you rescue, fix or try to control others, and where setting a boundary feels frightening. It is not a medical diagnosis, and it is learned, so it can be unlearned.

The statements here were written for cv.cm around common descriptions of codependency: people-pleasing, difficulty saying no, feeling responsible for others, needing approval and staying in hurtful situations. They are not taken from any published questionnaire and have not been validated, and half of them describe the opposite so that agreeing with everything lands in the middle. Use your score as a prompt for reflection; a counselor can help you sort out what it means for you.

faq.q: What are the signs of codependency?
faq.a: Common signs are trouble saying no, feeling guilty when you put yourself first, needing to be needed, trying to fix or rescue other people, a strong fear of being left, and staying in relationships that hurt you.

faq.q: How is the score worked out?
faq.a: Each statement scores 0 to 4, and half are reversed, so the total runs from 0 to 56. 18 or less shows few signs, 19 to 37 some and 38 or more many.

faq.q: Is codependency the same as being caring?
faq.a: No. Caring for someone is healthy when you can also look after yourself and say no. Codependency is when caring for others comes at the cost of your own needs, feelings and limits.

faq.q: How do I stop being codependent?
faq.a: Start small: notice what you feel and want, practice saying no to little requests, and let other people handle their own problems. Support groups such as Co-Dependents Anonymous (CoDA) and therapy, especially for setting boundaries, help many people.

items: I find it very hard to say no, even when I'm already stretched.
I can let other people deal with their own problems.
I feel responsible for how the people close to me feel.
I know what I want and I ask for it.
I feel guilty when I put my own needs first.
I'm fine if someone is disappointed in me for a while.
I need to be needed to feel good about myself.
I keep my own friends and hobbies when I'm in a relationship.
I've stayed in relationships that hurt me because I was afraid to be alone.
I can disagree with people I love without panicking.
I often try to fix or rescue the people around me.
I rarely change my plans to keep someone else happy.
I hide my real feelings to avoid upsetting anyone.
My mood stays fairly steady even when someone near me is upset.

low.name: Few codependent signs (0–18)
low.body: You seem able to care about people while still keeping your own needs and limits. You can say no, let others solve their problems and stay yourself in a relationship. Keep it up, and keep an eye out for the times, such as stress or a new relationship, when old people-pleasing habits can creep back in.

some.name: Some codependent patterns (19–37)
some.body: Some codependent habits show up in your life, perhaps with one person or in one area, such as work or family. That is very common. Try noticing the moments you say yes when you mean no, and practice small boundaries: a short pause before agreeing, an honest "I can't this time". Your needs count as much as anyone else's.

high.name: Many codependent signs (38–56)
high.body: Putting other people first seems to shape a lot of your life, often at the expense of your own feelings and wellbeing. You learned this for a reason, and you can learn other ways too. Talking to a counselor or therapist, or joining a group like Co-Dependents Anonymous (CoDA), can help you build boundaries and a sense of worth that doesn't depend on being needed.
